title: Alarm zone permanently open
summary: The zone never seals: the panel shows it open, in alarm, tamper or trouble all the time.
symptoms: Zone shows open / unsealed and the area can't be armed without isolating it.
Depending on the panel and EOL setup, it may be reported as alarm, tamper or trouble.
The fault stays when nobody is near the detector.
safety: Tell the monitoring centre and the site contact before testing, and put the system or zone into test/service mode under site procedure, to avoid false dispatches.
Photograph or label terminations before disconnecting anything.
Only measure resistance on an isolated circuit: disconnect the zone conductors from the panel first (and power down where the manufacturer requires). Never use the Ω range on live terminals.
Voltage checks are taken live on the DC volts range with the probes on the terminals only. Never bridge or short a supply output.

nodes.text: What EOL values is this zone set up for?
nodes.help: These are generic examples, not a manufacturer's values. The measurement steps assume equal seal and alarm resistors (alarm = twice the seal value).

answers.label: 2k2 / 2k2 dual EOL (2.2 kΩ sealed, 4.4 kΩ alarm)
answers.finding: Zone uses 2k2 / 2k2 dual EOL (expect 2.2 kΩ sealed).

answers.label: 10k / 10k dual EOL (10 kΩ sealed, 20 kΩ alarm)
answers.finding: Zone uses 10k / 10k dual EOL (expect 10 kΩ sealed).

nodes.text: What's the history of this zone?

answers.label: It worked, and there's been recent work on site (renovation, ceiling or cabling work, detector replaced)
answers.finding: Zone worked before; recent work on site.

answers.label: It worked, and nothing has changed that I know of
answers.finding: Zone worked before; no known changes.

answers.label: New installation, or the panel was recently programmed

nodes.text: What does the zone loop measure at the panel?

test.procedure: Isolate the zone: disconnect both zone conductors from the panel terminals. With the detector sealed (cover on, nobody moving in view), measure across the two conductors on the Ω range.
test.expected: About the seal value: 2.2 kΩ for 2k2 / 2k2, or 10 kΩ for 10k / 10k.

nodes.safety: Resistance range only on the disconnected conductors — never across live panel terminals.

ranges.label: Near 0 Ω
ranges.finding: Loop reads {value} at the panel: effectively a short, not open.

ranges.label: Below the seal value
ranges.finding: Loop reads {value} at the panel: lower than the seal value.

ranges.label: About the seal value
ranges.finding: Loop reads {value} at the panel: about the seal value — the field wiring looks healthy when isolated.

ranges.label: Between seal and alarm values
ranges.finding: Loop reads {value}: between the seal and alarm values.

ranges.label: About the alarm value
ranges.finding: Loop reads {value}: the alarm value — the detector is reporting alarm continuously.

ranges.label: Well above the alarm value
ranges.finding: Loop reads {value}: well above the alarm value.

ranges.label: OL / open circuit
ranges.finding: Loop reads {value} at the panel: open circuit.

nodes.text: What does the detector's own EOL network measure?

test.procedure: Leave the zone isolated. At the detector, disconnect the zone cable from the detector's terminals and measure across the detector's zone terminals (cover on, sealed). This splits the circuit into detector and cable.
test.expected: About the seal value. If it is, the open is in the cable or joints.

nodes.safety: The zone stays disconnected at the panel while you measure.

ranges.label: Below the seal value
ranges.finding: Detector side reads {value}: not the expected value.

ranges.label: About the seal value
ranges.finding: Detector side reads {value}: healthy — the open is in the cable or joints.

ranges.label: Above the seal value but not open
ranges.finding: Detector side reads {value}: not the expected value.

ranges.label: OL / open circuit
ranges.finding: Detector side reads {value}: open — the fault is at the detector.

skip.label: I can't get to the detector

nodes.text: What is the supply voltage at the detector?

test.procedure: Reconnect the zone. Live test on the DC volts range: measure across the detector's + and − supply terminals with the detector connected and powered.
test.expected: Within the detector's rated range. For a nominal 12 V detector this is typically about 10.5–14.5 V; check the detector's datasheet.

nodes.safety: Probes on the supply terminals only. Never bridge or short the supply.

ranges.label: 10.5–14.6 V (normal for 12 V)
ranges.finding: Detector supply reads {value}: normal for a 12 V detector.

ranges.label: Above 14.6 V
ranges.finding: Detector supply reads {value}: higher than a 12 V detector expects.

nodes.text: With the area cleared and nobody moving in view for a minute, does the zone stay in alarm?
nodes.help: Watch the detector's alarm LED (if enabled) and the zone status on the panel or keypad.

answers.label: Yes, still in alarm
answers.finding: Zone stays in alarm with the area clear.

answers.label: No, it sealed
answers.finding: Zone sealed once the area was clear.

nodes.title: Confirm the zone's EOL values first
nodes.summary: A reading can only be judged against the values this zone is meant to use.
verify: Check the zone's EOL type and values in the panel programming.
Check installation records or as-built documentation.
With the zone isolated and the detector disconnected, measure each EOL resistor on its own.
actions: Restart this guide once you know the expected sealed and alarm values.
escalate: If the site has no records and the panel programming isn't accessible, contact the installing company or the panel manufacturer's support.
notes: Panels use many combinations (e.g. 2k2/2k2, 4k7/2k2, 10k/10k). None is universally correct; the panel's documentation and programming decide.

nodes.title: The loop is shorted, not open
nodes.summary: Isolated, the loop reads near 0 Ω. Some panels report a short as tamper or trouble rather than 'short', which can look like an open zone.
verify: Follow the 'Alarm zone permanently shorted' guide to locate the short.
actions: Locate and repair the short before changing any programming.
notes: How a panel reports open, short and tamper depends on the manufacturer and the zone's programming.

nodes.title: The loop reads an unexpected value
nodes.summary: The isolated loop is neither sealed, alarm nor open. A wrong resistor or a poor joint is likely, but confirm by measuring the parts on their own.
verify: With the zone isolated and the detector disconnected, measure each EOL resistor on its own. Trust the meter over the colour bands.
Check every joint and termination for corrosion, loose screws or nicked conductors.
Confirm the panel is programmed for the EOL values actually fitted.
actions: Replace any resistor that doesn't measure the intended value.
Remake poor joints with suitable connectors.
Re-measure the loop (expect the seal value) before reconnecting.
escalate: If the readings drift or change when cables are moved, the fault may be intermittent — check the full cable run.

nodes.title: Field wiring looks healthy — check the panel end
nodes.summary: Isolated, the loop reads sealed, yet the panel reports the zone open. The likely cause is at the panel end, but verify before changing anything.
verify: Reconnect the conductors firmly on the correct zone terminals and re-check the zone status.
Check the zone's EOL type and values, zone type and zone number in the panel programming.
As a comparison, fit a known-good resistor of the seal value directly on the zone input (zone conductors disconnected) and see whether the panel shows it sealed.
actions: Correct terminations or programming as found.
If a known-good resistor on the input also shows open, move the zone to a spare input where the system design allows, and report the faulty input.
escalate: A zone input or expander that reads a known-good resistor incorrectly may be faulty — contact the manufacturer's technical support with the model and firmware version.

nodes.title: The open is at the detector
nodes.summary: The detector's own EOL network reads open, so the fault is most likely at the detector end.
verify: Check the detector cover is fully seated and the tamper switch is actuated.
With the cover off and the detector isolated, check the tamper switch for continuity when pressed.
Check the EOL resistors are fitted where the wiring diagram says and measure each one.
actions: Re-seat the cover or replace a faulty tamper switch / detector.
Replace an open resistor; re-terminate any loose conductor.
Re-measure at the detector, then at the panel, before reconnecting.
escalate: If the detector's internal contacts measure open with the detector powered and sealed, the detector may be faulty — replace it or contact the manufacturer.
notes: Many PIR alarm relays open when the detector is unpowered — measure with the detector powered if you suspect the relay.

nodes.title: The detector's EOL network reads the wrong value
nodes.summary: Measured on its own, the detector end isn't the seal value. Its wiring or resistors are likely wrong, but confirm part by part.
verify: Compare the detector wiring with the panel's and detector's wiring diagrams.
With the detector isolated, measure each EOL resistor on its own.
Check the tamper and alarm contacts are in the positions the diagram shows.
actions: Correct the wiring or replace the wrong resistor, then re-measure the detector end (expect the seal value).

nodes.title: The open is in the cable or joints
nodes.summary: The detector end reads healthy but the loop is open at the panel, so a conductor or joint in between is likely open.
verify: With the cable disconnected at both ends, join two cores at one end and measure the loop at the other: a good pair reads close to 0 Ω. Repeat for each core.
Inspect joints, junction boxes and any area where recent work was done.
actions: Repair or replace the faulty section; use a spare core only where it is sound and the change is recorded.
escalate: If the cable can't be traced or replaced safely (e.g. concealed in walls), quote a recable and record the temporary arrangement.

nodes.title: Open circuit between the panel and the detector
nodes.summary: The loop is open, but without testing at the detector the fault can't be placed in the cable or the detector.
verify: Get access to the detector and measure its EOL network with the cable disconnected.
Check continuity of each conductor end to end.
actions: Repair the faulty section once located.

nodes.title: The detector has no supply
nodes.summary: With no supply, many detectors hold their alarm relay open, so the zone reads alarm/open permanently.
verify: Measure the panel's AUX / detector supply output (DC volts, live) at the panel.
If the panel output is present, the supply conductors to the detector are likely open — check continuity with the cable isolated.
Check fuses or electronic protection on the AUX output and the total AUX load.
actions: Restore the supply (repair conductor, replace fuse, reduce overload) and re-test the zone.
escalate: Mains supply faults inside the panel must be handled by a licensed electrician where mains wiring is involved.

nodes.title: The detector supply is low
nodes.summary: A low supply can make detectors hold alarm or behave erratically.
verify: Compare the voltage at the panel AUX output with the voltage at the detector: a large difference points to voltage drop in the cable or joints.
Check the battery and charger, and the total AUX load against the panel's rating.
actions: Fix poor joints, use a heavier or doubled conductor for long runs, or add a supervised power supply where the load needs it.

nodes.title: The detector supply is higher than expected
nodes.summary: The supply is above the usual range for a 12 V detector. Check the detector's rating before going further.
verify: Check the detector's datasheet for its supply range.
Check which supply output the detector is connected to.
actions: Connect the detector to a supply within its rating; replace it if it has been damaged.

nodes.title: The detector is holding alarm
nodes.summary: The loop reads the alarm value and the detector doesn't reset with the area clear. The detector, or something in its view, is the likely cause.
verify: Look for heat sources, moving objects, insects or masking in the detector's field of view.
Check the detector's settings (sensitivity, anti-mask) against its manual.
Swap in a known-good detector to confirm.
actions: Remove the cause, re-site the detector or replace it if faulty.
escalate: If an anti-mask detector keeps reporting masking with a clear view, contact the manufacturer.

nodes.title: The fault isn't present now
nodes.summary: The zone sealed once the area was clear, so the detector was seeing movement. If the open returns, treat it as intermittent.
verify: Review the panel's event log for when the zone opens and closes.
Flex cables and joints gently while watching the zone status to find an intermittent connection.
actions: Remove false-alarm sources from the detector's view and remake any suspect joint.

nodes.title: Measurements needed
nodes.summary: Without measurements the possible causes can't be narrowed down safely.
verify: Get a multimeter: the next steps rely on isolated resistance and live voltage measurements.
Meanwhile, check the detector cover, LED and visible terminations.
actions: Return to this guide with a meter.

cable-damage.title: Damaged or broken cable
cable-damage.detail: A conductor cut, crushed or broken — by a staple, ceiling work or rodents — or a failed joint.

cable-short.title: Short in the cable
cable-short.detail: Conductors touching through damaged insulation, a staple or a poor joint.

wrong-termination.title: Loose or incorrect terminations
wrong-termination.detail: A conductor not clamped, on the wrong terminal, or a joint that has come apart.

detector-alarm.title: Detector stuck in alarm
detector-alarm.detail: The detector's alarm relay stays open: movement or heat sources in view, masking, or a faulty detector.

no-power.title: Detector not powered
no-power.detail: Many detectors' alarm relays open when unpowered, so a lost supply looks like a permanent alarm or open.

supply-fault.title: Supply fault
supply-fault.detail: Blown fuse or tripped protection, overloaded AUX output, flat battery or mains failure, or a broken power conductor.

wrong-supply.title: Wrong supply voltage
wrong-supply.detail: The detector is connected to a supply outside its rating (e.g. 24 V on a 12 V detector).

tamper-open.title: Tamper switch open
tamper-open.detail: Cover not seated or tamper switch faulty. In dual EOL the tamper is usually in series, so it opens the whole loop.

resistor-failed.title: EOL resistor open or missing
resistor-failed.detail: A resistor broken, burnt or not fitted where the wiring needs it.

wrong-resistor.title: Wrong resistor value
wrong-resistor.detail: A resistor of the wrong value fitted, so the loop reads outside the panel's expected bands.

hr-joint.title: High-resistance joint
hr-joint.detail: A corroded or poorly made joint adding resistance to the loop.

config.title: Programming doesn't match the wiring
config.detail: The zone's EOL type or values, zone type or zone number in the panel don't match what's installed.

panel-input.title: Panel zone input or expander fault
panel-input.detail: The input itself misreads a healthy loop.

escalation: Escalate to a senior technician or the manufacturer's technical support when a known-good resistor on the input doesn't read sealed, or readings are inconsistent.
Work on mains wiring inside panels or power supplies must be done by a licensed electrician.
If the zone must stay isolated, tell the site contact and monitoring centre, record it, and book the return visit.
notes: 2k2 / 4k4 and 10k / 20k are generic examples. Your panel's EOL values, and how it reports open, short and tamper, depend on the manufacturer, model and programming — check its documentation.
Resistance is only meaningful on an isolated circuit; a live zone input can give misleading Ω readings and can damage the meter.
